questions.q: What is the core failure mode of an approval checkpoint that has no escalation plan?
options: It approves every action automatically after one second
It doesn't fail safely — a pending request can just hang indefinitely if the assigned approver never responds
The Claude API automatically rejects it after 24 hours
It causes the agent to crash immediately
questions.explain: A single approver with no backup plan is a single point of failure: if they're unavailable, the request simply sits unanswered, which can itself cause damage (an unanswered ticket, a stalled process).

options: It immediately approves the action if no one responds within a second
It deletes the pending request after a fixed window
If the assigned approver hasn't responded within a set window, the request automatically routes to a different or broader set of reviewers
It disables the tool entirely after a timeout
questions.explain: Timeout escalation reassigns a stalled request to a second reviewer or a broader queue after a defined window, rather than leaving it indefinitely with one person.

questions.q: What is the idea behind tiered approval, as illustrated by requiring two independent approvers for a large wire transfer but one for a small refund?
options: All actions should always require exactly the same number of approvers regardless of risk
The number of required approvers should scale with the action's risk (amount, sensitivity), similar to a two-signature check in accounting
Tiered approval means only senior employees are ever allowed to approve anything
Tiered approval replaces the need for any timeout handling
questions.explain: Tiered approval matches scrutiny to risk: low-stakes approvals stay fast with one reviewer, while the highest-stakes actions require more independent sign-off before executing.

questions.q: When is "fallback to the safe default" an appropriate escalation pattern for a timed-out approval?
options: Always, for every tool, regardless of what the default outcome would be
Only when doing nothing or taking the conservative/reversible action is genuinely the safer option for that specific tool — not as a universal escape hatch
Never — it should only be used to approve the action automatically
Only for tools that have no real-world effect at all
questions.explain: Fallback to safe only works when the conservative default really is lower-risk for that tool (e.g., not auto-renewing is safer than an unwanted renewal); it requires the same risk judgment used to decide a tool needed approval in the first place.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should an agent do while a tool call is stuck waiting on human approval?
options: Immediately retry the exact same tool call in a tight loop until it succeeds
Terminate the entire session with no explanation
Report status back to the user, continue independent sub-tasks that don't depend on the pending approval, and eventually time out the overall task if nothing can proceed
Silently proceed with the action anyway after a few seconds
questions.explain: A well-built loop treats a pending approval as its own state rather than freezing entirely — it can keep the user informed, make progress elsewhere, and eventually give up on the whole task if nothing can move forward.
